title: Because, so, although — linking your reasons
goal: Join two ideas the way Indonesians do: give a reason (*karena, soalnya*), a result (*jadi, sehingga, makanya*), a purpose (*supaya, agar, biar*) and a contrast (*meskipun, walaupun, padahal*) — in both the written and the spoken register.
bekal: explain why something happened: *Mesinnya rusak, sehingga modulnya belum dicetak*
say what something is for: *Aku mau beli motor supaya nggak tergantung ojek*
concede and complain: *Meskipun mahal, kita tetap pesan* and *Padahal sudah jam tiga!*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kenapa belum jadi?
dialogs.intro: Late January. The office is running a training day for teachers from its partner schools next week, and the printed handbooks are nowhere to be seen. Sarah asks Mas Bayu what has happened.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Mas, modul pelatihan untuk sekolah mitra kok belum jadi? Padahal acaranya minggu depan.
lines.id: Bayu, how come the training handbooks for the partner schools aren't ready? The event's next week, you know.
lines.literal: brother, module training for school partner [kok] not-yet done? whereas event-the week front.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Iya, Mbak, maaf. Ada beberapa masalah, jadi semuanya mundur.
lines.id: Yes, sorry. There were a few problems, so everything's slipped.
lines.literal: yes, miss, sorry. exist several problem, so all-of-it back-off.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Masalah apa saja? Coba ceritakan pelan-pelan.
lines.id: What sort of problems? Tell me, slowly.

lines.text: Desainernya sakit tiga hari, sehingga desainnya baru selesai kemarin.

lines.text: Walaupun lebih mahal, kita tetap harus tepat waktu. Guru-guru sudah menunggu.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Betul juga. Kalau begitu, aku pesan di sana hari ini, supaya selesai hari Kamis.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke. Aku minta persetujuan anggaran ke Mbak Nur, biar dia nggak kaget.

lines.literal: OK. I ask approval budget to miss Nur, let she not startled.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Makasih, Mbak. Aku kira Mbak bakal marah.
lines.id: Thanks. I thought you'd be angry.
lines.literal: thanks, miss. I thought miss will angry.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Aku nggak marah. Aku cuma kesal karena baru tahu sekarang.
lines.id: I'm not angry. I'm just annoyed because I've only just found out.
lines.literal: I not angry. I only annoyed because just know now.

lines.speaker: Bayu:
lines.text: Iya, harusnya aku bilang dari minggu lalu. Lain kali aku langsung lapor, deh.
lines.id: Yes, I should have told you last week. Next time I'll tell you straight away, promise.

notes: **Padahal — "and yet, even though".** It adds a fact that makes the situation worse or more surprising, and it usually comes **after** the main statement: *Modulnya belum jadi. Padahal acaranya minggu depan.* It is the complaint word: there is almost always a sigh in it. It is not a neutral "although" — for that, see *meskipun* below.

**Jadi and sehingga** both introduce a result. *Jadi* ("so") is everyday and can start a sentence. *Sehingga* ("so that, with the result that") is careful and written, and sits in the middle of one sentence, joining cause to result. Bayu uses it because he is explaining himself to his coordinator and wants to sound organised.

**Mundur — "slipped, went back".** *Mundur* is to move backwards; for schedules it means "postponed, delayed": *Jadwalnya mundur seminggu* (the schedule has slipped a week). The opposite is *maju*: *Rapatnya maju jam satu* (the meeting has been brought forward to one).

**Percetakan langganan.** *Langganan* is a subscription, and by extension your regular supplier or customer: *warung langganan* (your usual warung), *tukang ojek langganan* (your regular ojek driver). Being someone's *langganan* is a relationship, and it earns you small favours.

**Biar and bakal** 💬 are the spoken twins of *supaya* (so that) and *akan* (will). *Biar dia nggak kaget* = *supaya dia tidak kaget*. You would not write either in a report, but you will hear them fifty times a day.

**Kesal, not marah.** *Marah* is openly angry, and in a Javanese office showing it is a loss of face for everyone. *Kesal* is "annoyed, fed up" — an honest feeling you can admit to calmly. Sarah's line is a model of saying something critical without raising the temperature.

grammars.title: Because and so
body: The reason words go in front of the reason; the result words go in front of the result. Each has a register, and choosing the right one is half of sounding natural.

head: Word
Job
Register
Example
rows: so that, with the result that

after: *Soalnya* starts a new sentence that explains the previous one — it is how people really give reasons in conversation. *Makanya* can also be a gentle told-you-so: *Makanya, bawa payung!* (That's why you should take an umbrella!)
⚠️ *Karena hujan, jadi aku telat* — reason word and result word in the same sentence — is extremely common in speech, but a teacher will cross out one of them in writing. Use one or the other.

grammars.title: Although, even though
body: *Meskipun* and *walaupun* are the neutral "although" and are interchangeable. The main clause often adds *tetap* (still) to underline that the fact didn't change anything.

head: Word
Register
Example
English
rows: Although it's expensive, the result is good.
Even in the rain the market is busy.
Even though it's far, I'm still going.
He's still hungry, even though he's eaten.
However, the result is not yet satisfactory.

after: ⚠️ *Meskipun mahal, tapi hasilnya bagus* — with both *meskipun* and *tapi* — is what many Indonesians say, and what every editor deletes. Keep *meskipun* and replace *tapi* with *tetap* if you want the extra push.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Beli motor atau tidak?
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning. Bu Endang is sweeping the lane outside her gate when Sarah comes out with a list of second-hand motorbike ads on her phone.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Mbak Sarah jadi beli motor, to?
lines.id: So you're buying a motorbike after all, are you?
lines.literal: miss Sarah go-ahead buy motorbike, [to]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Masih bingung, Bu. Soalnya saya belum pernah naik motor sendiri di Indonesia.
lines.id: I still can't decide. The thing is, I've never ridden one myself in Indonesia.
lines.literal: still confused, madam. the-matter-is I not-yet ever ride motorbike self in Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Lho, jalanan Jogja nggak seramai Jakarta. Pelan-pelan pasti bisa.
lines.id: Oh, Yogya's roads aren't as busy as Jakarta's. Take it slowly and you'll be fine.
lines.literal: [lho], roads Jogja not as-busy Jakarta. slow-slow surely can.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Iya, sih. Supaya nggak tergantung ojek, memang lebih baik punya motor sendiri.
lines.id: True. If I don't want to depend on ojeks, it's better to have my own bike.
lines.literal: yes, [sih]. so-that not dependent ojek, indeed more good have motorbike self.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Betul. Naik ojek tiap hari itu mahal, padahal motor bekas harganya nggak seberapa.
lines.id: Exactly. Ojeks every day add up, and a second-hand bike doesn't cost much at all.
lines.literal: correct. ride ojek every day that expensive, whereas motorbike used price-its not how-much.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tapi saya harus bikin SIM dulu, supaya nggak ditilang polisi.
lines.id: But I have to get a licence first, so the police don't fine me.
lines.literal: but I must make licence first, so-that not is-ticketed police.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Gampang. Nanti minta tolong Mas Bayu antar ke kantor polisi.
lines.id: That's easy. Ask Bayu to take you to the police station.
lines.literal: easy. later ask help brother Bayu escort to office police.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Meskipun begitu, saya tetap agak takut, Bu.
lines.id: Even so, I'm still a bit scared.
lines.literal: although like-that, I still rather afraid, madam.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Wajar, Mbak. Latihan dulu di lapangan dekat masjid, pagi-pagi, pas masih sepi.
lines.id: That's natural. Practise on the field by the mosque first, early in the morning when it's quiet.
lines.literal: natural, miss. practice first at field near mosque, morning-morning, exactly still quiet.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke, Bu. Saya latihan dulu, jadi kalau sudah berani, baru saya beli.
lines.id: All right. I'll practise first, and once I'm confident, then I'll buy one.
lines.literal: OK, madam. I practice first, so if already brave, only-then I buy.

lines.speaker: Endang:
lines.text: Nah, gitu. Dimas pasti senang, soalnya dia bisa minta dibonceng.
lines.id: That's the way. Dimas will be thrilled, because he can ask for rides on the back.
lines.literal: [nah], like-that. Dimas surely happy, the-matter-is he can ask be-carried-pillion.

notes: **Jadi beli motor, to?** Two things here. *Jadi* + verb means "go ahead with, actually do (what was planned)": *Jadi ke Dieng?* (Is the Dieng trip still on?), *Nggak jadi* (it's off). And *to* is the Yogyakarta tag "isn't it, aren't you" — Javanese, warm, and a sign that the speaker assumes you agree.

**Soalnya** 💬 literally "its matter", is how people actually say "because" in conversation: first the statement, then *soalnya* and the explanation. Sarah uses it with Bu Endang — polite (*saya*, *Bu*) but not office-formal.
**Iya, sih — "true, I suppose".** *Sih* softens the agreement and hints that there is a "but" coming. It is the sound of someone being persuaded against their better judgement.

**Nggak seberapa — "not much at all".** *Seberapa* is "how much"; negated, it means "hardly anything": *Gajinya nggak seberapa* (the pay is nothing special). It is also the modest reply to a compliment on a gift: *Ah, nggak seberapa, Bu.*

**SIM and ditilang.** *SIM* (*Surat Izin Mengemudi*) is a driving licence — *SIM C* for motorbikes, *SIM A* for cars. *Tilang* (from *bukti pelanggaran*, "proof of violation") is a traffic ticket; *ditilang* is being stopped and fined. Foreign residents with a KITAS can apply for a SIM; bring your passport and KITAS.

**Baru — "only then"** — after a condition: *Kalau sudah berani, baru saya beli* (once I'm confident, then — and not before — I'll buy). **Dibonceng** is riding pillion; *membonceng* is giving someone a ride on the back. In Yogya, a ten-year-old's whole social life depends on it.

grammars.title: So that: untuk, supaya, agar, biar
body: *Untuk* is followed by a verb or a noun; *supaya, agar* and *biar* are followed by a whole clause, often with its own subject.
after: ⚠️ Don't stack them: *untuk supaya* is a classic learner (and native) redundancy. One is enough.
💬 In speech a negative purpose is often just *nanti* or *ntar* — "or else": *Pakai jaket, nanti masuk angin* (put a jacket on or you'll catch a chill).

sections.title: Connecting ideas: one map, two registers

blocks.text: Every connector in this unit has a spoken and a written form. In a WhatsApp message to a friend use the right-hand column; in an email to a partner school use the middle one.
*Gara-gara* is "because of" with a finger pointed: *Gara-gara kamu, kita telat!* (Thanks to you, we're late!). Use it for bad causes only, and preferably with a smile.
*Padahal* sets what happened against what should have happened. English uses tone of voice, *even though*, *and yet* or *considering*; Indonesian packs it into one word. Learn it through examples.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: *Kok belum makan? Padahal sudah jam tiga.*
Why haven't you eaten? It's three o'clock!
He didn't come, even though he promised.
The price went up, and the quality's the same.
*Aku kira dia orang Jawa, padahal dari Medan.*
I thought he was Javanese, but actually he's from Medan.
Still tired, considering I slept ten hours.
And it was only for a moment, too.

blocks.title: Classic mistakes in written Indonesian
items: ⚠️ *Meskipun hujan, tapi dia datang.* → *Meskipun hujan, dia tetap datang.*
⚠️ *Karena hujan, jadi acara batal.* → *Karena hujan, acara batal.*
⚠️ *Sehingga* at the start of a sentence → join it to the sentence before.
